messages.subject: Interpretations of the results of mixed logit models
messages.subject_clean: Interpretations of the results of mixed logit models
messages.body_plain:
Dear researchers



I have conducted experiments of English-to-English structural priming in
sentence production. The following is the descriptions of my analyses using
mixed logit models.



The participants’ responses (Active or Passive) were fit using mixed logit
models with Group (Native speakers vs. L2 speakers), Prime Type (Active,
Passive, Unergative-intransitive, or Unaccusative-intransitive), and the
two-way interaction between them as fixed factors, and participants and
items as random effects. Treatment coding was used to represent Group and
Prime Type.



I obtained a significant effect of Group; L2 speakers produced more passive
target responses than native speakers. I also obtained a significant effect
of Prime Type; native speakers produced more passive target responses
following passive primes than following active primes. (Note that the
active prime condition in the L1 group was taken as the reference level.)
Most importantly, there was no interaction between Group and Prime Type.
The absence of the interaction suggests that structural priming was present
in both native speakers and L2 speakers. (The coefficient associated with
the interaction was negative, indicating that the effect of structural
priming was *numerically* smaller in L2 speakers than in native speakers.)



Because the two-way interaction was not significant, we will usually stop
here. However, I wanted to examine the effect of L2 proficiency on
structural priming in the bilingual group. (and of course, there are no
L2-proficiency scores for native speakers of English.) So I performed
separate analyses. Specifically, I analyzed L2 speakers target responses
using mixed logit models with Prime Type, L2-proficiency, and the
interaction between them as fixed factors and participants and items as
random effects. Treatment coding was used to represent Prime Type. The
L2-proficiency variable was centered to its mean.



When I performed this separate analysis focusing on L2 speakers’ target
responses, the effect of Prime Type was not significant. (The interaction
between Prime Type and L2-proficiency was not significant, either. There
was no effect of L2-proficiency.)



How should I interpret this kind of data pattern? Why did the separate
analysis fail to obtain an effect of Prime Type in the bilingual group
(i.e., L2 speakers), when there was no interaction between Group and Prime
Type in the overall analyses?



I originally concluded that “the L2 group differed from the L1 group;
structural priming was present in native speakers but not in L2 speakers.”
However, because the interaction between Group and Prime Type did not reach
significance in the overall analysis, my interpretation seems problematic...



Does anyone have feedback or comments on how I should interpret such a data
pattern and/or why such a data pattern may be obtained?



Thank you very much for any feedback/comments you may have in advance!


Best regards,

Sunfa Kim

messages.subject_clean: Interpretations of the results of mixed logit models
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sunfa Kim,

This is a pretty common situation. To understand it, it's important to
remember that a non-significant effect does not mean the effect is absent;
there is simply not enough evidence to reject the possibility that it is
absent.

In your data, there's not enough evidence to reject the hypothesis that L2
speakers are sensitive to prime type. However, that  statements is
consistent with the possibility that there is, in fact, an effect in this
condition -- you simply don't have enough evidence to decide one way or the
other.

The interaction test is therefore critical in this context. It asks: is
there sufficient evidence to reject the hypothesis that the two groups show
the same effect of prime type? The answer here is no.

There's a nice discussion of the issue in this paper (and the failure of
lots of researchers to attend to it):
http://www.nature.com/doifinder/10.1038/nn.2886

hth,
mG

messages.subject: Comparing two groups who received some but not all of the same items
messages.subject_clean: Comparing two groups who received some but not all of the same items
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Is it possible to compare group A and B responses in a mixed-effects linear
model if the items that each group saw were not 100% the same? Each group
saw mostly overlapping items (~200 items) but some distinct items (~100
items). Since I am interested in the group difference, can I treat items as
a random effect in such a model? Is there any concern that the group
differences may be driven by either the overlapping or the distinct items
only?

SJ
